Marathon Petroleum fell slightly today despite continued strength in global oil prices, which hit a six-month high above $116 as Middle East tensions escalated and the U.S. signaled potential military action against Iran. The stock has actually declined about $19 from its October 16 peak, even as crude prices have climbed—suggesting that refiner profit margins may be tightening faster than higher oil prices can offset. Refineries are running at 93.4% capacity with healthy fuel inventories, so the headwind isn't coming from weak demand or operations.

The disconnect highlights a key risk for refiners in this environment: when crude oil prices spike due to geopolitical crisis rather than demand strength, refiners often see their margins squeezed. Higher crude costs are passed through to gasoline and diesel prices more slowly, leaving less spread between what refiners buy and sell. Additionally, concerns about a widening Middle East conflict and potential disruptions to global oil supply may be pricing in scenarios where crude becomes so expensive that fuel demand weakens—which would hurt refiners more than pure oil traders.
